blindSummary: The equality watchdog's updated Code of Practice for services, public functions and associations was laid 21 May 2026 and came into force on 5 August 2026 as statutory guidance (replacing the 2011 code): single-sex spaces open to the public - toilets, gym changing rooms, hospital wards, rape-crisis centres - should be organised by biological sex, with trans people directed to gender-neutral or birth-sex facilities. The guidance binds service providers across the whole country but is administered in this unit. Its legal predicate is a top-court ruling (16 April 2025): 'sex' and 'woman' in the 2010 equality statute mean biological/registered sex, and a gender-recognition certificate does not change legal sex for its purposes. The ruling has immediate visitor-facing consequences in this unit's transport and custody settings: following it, the rail-network police moved (17 April 2025, stated interim position) to strip-searching trans women detained on the rail network by male officers, reversing the acquired-gender policy for certificate holders. Anti-trans offending is statistically invisible in the official record: crime statistics covering this unit and one neighbouring unit reported 115,990 hate crimes in the year to March 2025 across five monitored strands, and transgender identity is not a separately recorded strand (it is recorded separately in two other units of the country). Practical variation inside the unit is concentrated in the capital - visible community, dedicated services, dedicated hate-crime policing - versus the rest of the unit; no sourced sub-unit region-level evidence was found, so the unit is assessed whole.
blindSourceSummaries: A national broadcaster (19 June 2026): a judge ruled the prison service of one constituent unit's guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful - sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the top court's April 2025 definition-of-a-woman ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same countrywide ruling imposes on this unit's prison and custody decisions; that unit's government said it would consider the judgment (the top court had already held that the human-rights convention confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

A national broadcaster (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while a campaign group called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the top court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for this unit's equality-watchdog code and rail-police strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation countrywide.

A national newspaper (17 April 2025): the rail-network police amended its custody strip-searching policy after the top court's gender ruling - same-sex searches in custody now to be 'undertaken in accordance with the biological birth sex of the detainee', meaning trans people arrested on the national rail network are strip-searched by male officers; the previous policy searched certificate holders by acquired gender. The force called it an 'interim position while we digest yesterday's judgment' - a direct, visitor-facing practice change.
